section_summary: This section consists of newspaper clippings enclosed with the American Embassy at Lima’s despatch no. 245, documenting the Peruvian press controversy over Japanese immigration and economic activity. Early items warn of Japanese control of land, commerce, industry and employment, including an alleged attempt to evict yanacona families from Hacienda Ansieta. Later advertisements and statements by Japanese community leaders defend the immigrants’ contributions to Peruvian agriculture and small business, praise Peru’s prosperity, and advocate closer Peru–Japan trade relations.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 46: “La Infiltración Japonesa”
subfiles.about: An opinion article endorsing La Prensa’s campaign against perceived Japanese economic infiltration in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Brenner Acha argues that Japanese ownership of farms, factories, industries and schools threatens to reduce Peruvians to employees of Japanese proprietors. While praising Japanese industry and patriotism and acknowledging a few assimilated families, he contends that most immigrants preserve a separate “little Japan” and urges Peruvians to defend their own land and economic opportunities.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 47: “La Voz de los Lectores”
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping — letters to the editor
subfiles.from: D. M. García; Samuel Enrique Gómez V.
subfiles.about: Two readers congratulate La Prensa for its campaign against Japanese economic and demographic influence.
subfiles.summary: D. M. García praises articles by Jorge Badani and Salinas Cossio as patriotic contributions to national policy. Samuel Enrique Gómez V. alleges that Japanese residents have monopolized industries, commerce and land, and calls for legal measures limiting the citizenship rights of their Peru-born children. He warns that continued immigration could eventually permit Japanese political control of Peru.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 48: “La Actividad Japonesa en el Perú”
subfiles.about: An editorial assesses the newspaper’s debate over Japanese participation in Peruvian agriculture, commerce and society.
subfiles.summary: The editorial characterizes the recent debate as a sober warning rather than a campaign of anti-Japanese prejudice. It identifies landholding and the displacement of Peruvian artisans and small traders as the most serious concerns, while rejecting unnecessary obstacles to legitimate Peru–Japan commerce. It argues that enforcement of Peruvian laws, national economic solidarity and fair competition can prevent conflict and preserve friendly relations.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 49: “Ocúpase de la infiltración japonesa en el Perú un ex-director de Fomento”
subfiles.from: La Crónica, reporting statements by Enrique Zegarra
subfiles.about: A report summarizes Enrique Zegarra’s claims about Japanese immigration, economic competition and government assistance.
subfiles.summary: Zegarra asserts that 22,560 of Peru’s 48,317 registered foreigners are Japanese and that continued arrivals worsen unemployment among Peruvian workers. He alleges that Japanese government support facilitates settlement and that Japanese competition has displaced local producers in Cusco, Huánuco, Junín and Loreto. He also alleges exclusion of Peruvian laborers in the Chancay Valley and recommends close government scrutiny of Lima Nippo and Perú Jiho.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 50: “Los tentáculos del pulpo nipón han aprisionado esta vez a más de doscientos yanaconas nacionales”
subfiles.about: A report alleges that a Japanese firm’s purchase of Hacienda Ansieta threatened more than two hundred yanacona families with eviction.
subfiles.summary: The article says a Japanese firm used a fixer known as Manteca to obtain eviction orders, including one against Anselma Ramírez, widow of Mamani. It accuses the Vitarte justice of the peace of continuing proceedings despite a jurisdictional challenge and of falsely reporting that the affected parcels lacked houses, crops and fruit trees. Pablo Toledo, Julia de los Ríos and other residents planned to seek civil and criminal sanctions against the judge.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 51: Christmas and New Year greeting from the Sociedad Central Japonesa del Perú
subfiles.about: The Japanese Central Society of Peru offers Christmas and New Year greetings to the Peruvian people.
subfiles.summary: The brief display advertisement wishes Peruvians a happy Christmas and a prosperous New Year. It presents the Japanese community organization in a cordial and publicly patriotic manner amid the broader press controversy.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 52: Christmas and New Year advertisements by Japanese merchants and industrialists
subfiles.from: Japanese merchants and industrialists in Lima and Callao
subfiles.about: A multi-page advertisement conveys holiday greetings and lists numerous Japanese-owned businesses and proprietors.
subfiles.summary: The advertisement promotes restaurants, cafés, hotels, laundries, bakeries, workshops and other Japanese-owned establishments in Lima, Miraflores and Callao. It supplies proprietors’ names and street addresses while wishing readers a happy Christmas and prosperous New Year. The spread documents the Japanese community’s extensive participation in urban small business.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 54: Fragmentary New Year greeting advertisement
subfiles.about: A fragment of a New Year advertisement contains only a partially legible commercial greeting.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure heading identifies the item as a La Crónica clipping of January 1, 1938. Only the words of a formulaic greeting are recoverable, and the advertiser’s identity and the remainder of the message are illegible in this section.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 55: “Saludo del Presidente de la Sociedad Central Japonesa del Perú”
subfiles.about: The president of the Japanese Central Society defends Japanese immigrants’ contributions to Peruvian agriculture and small industry.
subfiles.summary: Kurotobi praises Peru’s prosperity under Oscar R. Benavides and portrays Japan’s war in Asia as a defense against communism. Drawing on his own arrival as an agricultural laborer in 1901, he describes Japanese immigration, mortality, settlement patterns and the movement of former farmworkers into cafés, barbershops, shops, bakeries, bazaars and other trades. He argues that Japanese farmers improved coastal estates and that Japanese businesses employed Peruvians, lowered prices and expanded services without displacing national workers. The address closes with expressions of gratitude and loyalty to Peru as the immigrants’ second homeland.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 56: “Nuestra Misión en el Fomento de las Relaciones Económicas Peruano-Japonesas”
subfiles.about: The president of the Japanese Association of Commerce and Industry advocates collaboration and expanded trade between Peru and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi outlines the association’s goals of linking Japanese merchants, industrialists and farmers with Peruvian producers and markets. He stresses Japanese firms’ employment of Peruvians, low-price retailing, agricultural productivity and interest in establishing new industries, while denying central or Japanese-government financing of immigrant businesses. He argues that Japan needs Peruvian cotton, wool and minerals, notes Peru’s favorable trade balance, and proposes a Peruvian economic mission to Japan. The article presents commercial cooperation as a means of strengthening both Peru’s economy and bilateral friendship.

subfiles.title: Enclosure 57: “Saludo del Presidente de la Sociedad Central Japonesa del Perú con motivo del Año Nuevo”
subfiles.to: Readers of El Universal and the Peruvian public
subfiles.about: El Universal reprints Kurotobi’s New Year defense of Japanese immigration, agriculture and small business.
subfiles.summary: The reprint praises Peruvian order and prosperity, defends Japan’s actions in Asia as anti-communist, and recounts the history and demographic distribution of Japanese immigrants in Peru. It describes their early agricultural contracts, movement into urban trades, employment of Peruvians and claimed improvements to cafés, barbershops, retail stores and other enterprises. The text also praises Japanese farmers’ cultivation practices and presents the community as grateful to Peru; the article continues beyond the end of this section.
